newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Products Outlook - gasoline tied to stocks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Products Outlook - gasoline tied to stocks.

text.p: Refined product traders said they were keeping close tabs on the gasoline supply situation in the short term, though few players were calling for a sharp increase in prices.

Outright New York Harbor spot conventional unleaded gasoline prices sat at about 58.25 cents a gallon as of Friday, down abut 15 cents from the year-ago level, while U.S. Gulf prices sat at about 58.60 cents, down about 12 cents.
Market watchers said whether the prices surge higher ahead of the peak summer demand season will depend mostly on the state of U.S. inventories.

Cargill Investor Services' trader Thomas Blakeslee predicted new weekly American Petroleum Institute inventory data due out Tuesday will show a small decrease in U.S. gasoline stocks. U.S. gasoline stocks sat at 196 million barrels in last week's report, nearly 5.8 million barrels below the previous year's mark.

He said such a draw in this week's report, coupled with increasing demand as the driving season approaches, could likely push May NYMEX futures values up to 63.50 cents a gallon -- versus the 61.07 cent settlement price seen last Friday.

But Ken Miller, a senior analyst for Houston consulting firm Purvin & Gertz Inc, cautioned gasoline inventories will likely swell in the next few weeks from increased production runs and strong imports -- preventing differentials from widening much beyond current levels.

"We will have a firming move on gasoline as part of a seasonal pattern, but just moderately," he said, citing "dramatically higher" crude production runs in recent weeks now that earlier-than-usual maintenance turnarounds are complete.
He cited Dept of Energy data showing Gulf Coast crude runs of over 6.9 million barrels per day for the week ending April 4, compared with 6.5 million barrels the same week last year.

"It's quite an impressive increase, especially when you consider last year was a record year for the region," Miller said. Total U.S. crude runs "are now up to 94.2 percent versus 93.7 percent last year," he added.

"With that kind of increase, gasoline production will continue to rise," he said, as refiners maximize output to take advantage of current healthy margins, the return they see on product sales versus their crude oil costs.
"They'll run too much and destroy the margins because there's too much capacity," he said, predicting refinery margins may have already peaked weeks ahead of the normal seasonal trend.
As for distillates, Miller predicted differentials will hold fairly steady in the near term as refineries continue to maximize gasoline production at the expense of distillate output.
In the Midwest, traders expected unleaded gasoline basis to hold its ground after moving higher last week, leaving prices to track the underlying NYMEX unleaded futures contract.
"It's very strong right now, and it should stay fairly stable," one trader active in the Group Three and Chicago spot markets said of the unleaded basis. "The market is trying to hold here."
Spot diesel prices in the Midwest markets were expected to move lower this week after surging higher in recent days on perceptions of tighter supplies in the Gulf Coast market, traders said.
Overall, trade was expected to be thin through Tuesday while some players attended an industry gathering in Arizona.
